unit_label: Module B unit 3 (courseware unit 12), part 1: human behaviour and individual differences, personality, diversity and gender issues

facts.statement: Human behaviour is a complex combination of originating and responding behaviour and reflects the psychological structure of a person; it is the result of biological, psychological and social processes. Employee behaviour is the way employees respond to specific circumstances or situations at work, shaped by culture and by the organisation's culture. According to Kurt Lewin, behaviour is a function of the person and the environment around him, and neither explains behaviour alone. The courseware groups the factors influencing behaviour as: environmental (economic, social including norms and cultural values, and political); personal (age, sex, education, abilities, marital status, family background and other demographic factors); organisational (nature of the job, organisation structure and design, leadership, compensation and reward system, growth opportunities); and psychological (personality, perception, attitudes, values, learning).

The economic environment (level of employment, wage rates, economic outlook), culture (work ethic, achievement needs, values) and the stability and quality of the political system influence individual behaviour; so do personal characteristics, and organisational factors such as structure, physical facilities, reward system, personnel policies, culture and the quality of leadership. Because individuals differ, they must be treated differently in terms of their needs and motives. Managers have viewed employees as the "economic man" and "rational man" (motivated mainly by money); the Hawthorne studies showed that man is also a social being and led to the "social man" idea; this too was seen as simplistic, since it neglects the work itself and can be manipulative, and Argyris, Likert and McGregor argued that people need opportunities to use their creativity. The current thinking is to accept man as a complex being and to recognise that personalities differ; understanding personality helps managers predict behaviour such as absenteeism, turnover and work involvement and take timely preventive measures.

The technical competence of an individual matters, but behaviour and interpersonal skills are extremely important because people work in teams; team-building skills founded on individual behaviour and interpersonal skills yield synergy. The basic assumptions about human behaviour at work are: individuals differ; the concept of the whole person; behaviour is caused; an individual has dignity; organisations are social systems; there is mutuality of interest among organisational members; and organisational behaviour is holistic (the first four concern people, the next two organisations, and the last combines the first six). Every person is in certain respects like all other persons, like some other persons and like no other person.

Personality is defined (Salvatore Maddi) as a stable set of characteristics and tendencies that determine the commonalities and differences in the psychological behaviour (thoughts, feelings and actions) of people that have continuity in time; changes occur slowly over an extended period. According to Raymond Cattell, personality is a pattern of traits that helps to understand and predict behaviour; traits are permanent. Eysenck focused on temperaments, which he believed were largely controlled by genetic influences, and used factor analysis to identify two primary dimensions of personality: extraversion and neuroticism. Type A behaviour (described by Friedman, Meyer and Rosenman) is restless, impatient, multitasking, tries to schedule more and more in less and less time, often does not complete one thing before starting another and has no time to relax; Type B is easy going, relaxed about time pressure, less competitive, systematic and methodical, and has a balanced outlook on life.

Erikson's eight developmental stages of personality, with the courseware's workplace parallel: trust versus mistrust (dependence on others for guidance), autonomy versus shame and doubt (working independently after induction; doubting one's competence after mistakes), initiative versus guilt (taking initiative; guilt if things go wrong), industry versus inferiority (working hard to find a place; low self-esteem if unsuccessful), identity versus role confusion (proving oneself as an independent, effective adult), intimacy versus isolation (close relationships or isolation), generativity versus stagnation (developing others, and stagnation if not) and integrity versus despair (approaching retirement with a sense of self-worth or of purposelessness).

Personality theories in the courseware: the psychoanalytic theory (Freud) holds that personality has an id (the unconscious foundation, driven by pleasure and instincts and demanding immediate gratification), an ego (conscious, controlling the id through the realities of the external world) and a super ego (the conscience, the higher-level restraining force absorbing cultural and ethical values); a balance among the three is needed for a normal personality (an overdeveloped super ego makes a person feel guilty over little things, an underdeveloped one lets the id loose); trait theory holds that traits determining personality are basically inherent (more heredity than environment), for example aggressive, loyal, flexible, submissive; self-concept theory (Carl Rogers) holds that behaviour is consistent with the image one has of oneself, formed through interaction with the environment and reinforced by positive feedback and lowered by negative feedback; and social learning theory holds that personality is more a result of social variables than biological factors, learned through reinforcement and punishment, with behaviour and the environment affecting each other.

The courseware says the brain influences personality through electrical stimulation of the brain (ESB) and split-brain psychology. It tabulates the left hemisphere (controlling the right side of the body) with speech and verbal, logical and mathematical, linear and detailed, sequential, controlled, intellectual, analytic abilities, and the right hemisphere (controlling the left side) with spatial and musical, holistic, artistic and symbolic, simultaneous, emotional, intuitive and creative, synthetic and gestalt-oriented abilities and facial recognition, noting that these dimensions remain open for research. John Holland's personality-job fit theory proposes that satisfaction and dissatisfaction depend on how well an individual's personality matches the occupation, with six types: realistic (physical activities; shy, stable, practical; mechanic, farmer), investigative (thinking and understanding; analytical, curious; biologist, economist), social (helping others; sociable, friendly; social worker, teacher), conventional (rule-regulated, orderly; conforming, efficient, unimaginative; accountant, bank teller, file clerk), enterprising (verbal activities to influence others; self-confident, ambitious, domineering; lawyer, public relations specialist) and artistic (ambiguous, unsystematic creative activities; imaginative, disorderly, idealistic, emotional; painter, musician, writer).

Race or ethnicity and gender are the most recognised forms of workforce diversity; others include disability, family background, age, lifestyle and culture. Traditional HR systems are based on models of homogeneity: recruitment emphasises sources that produced successful candidates in the past, and decision-makers tend to hire, promote and evaluate people like themselves ("homogeneous reproduction"), allowing through only those who fit the dominant coalition. Aptitude tests for mass selection pick candidates with similar abilities, which becomes a problem when a competence becomes obsolete (the courseware's example: the numerical ability banks recruited for in the 1970s and 1980s became obsolete after computerisation, when selling and marketing skills were needed). Heterogeneous and complementary skills benefit organisations; managed well, workgroup diversity enhances creativity, problem solving, cohesiveness and communication and improves performance and quality of product and service. Realising the benefits has been elusive because diversity management has been introduced piecemeal, without a holistic view or integration with other systems, and legislation has been enacted without changing culture and beliefs.

The three predominant traditional HR approaches to diversity are: diversity enlargement (increasing the representation of individuals of different ethnic and cultural backgrounds by changing the demographic composition, on the assumption that diversity and exposure improve performance); diversity sensitivity (acknowledging cultural distance and teaching members about cultural differences through training, to promote communication and understanding); and the cultural audit (surveys to find what blocks the progress of non-traditional employees and how groups see the predominant culture, which fails if not linked to HR systems and should also find similarities between groups). Problems in achieving diversity: the "critical mass" issue (a few diverse workers may feel isolated or tokens, Kanter 1977); it takes considerable time before the organisation's demographic profile reflects its efforts; and business conditions (growth and frequent hiring make it faster, slow or no expansion or downsizing makes it difficult).

Gender issues: jobs have preferences for a gender for physical, social, psychological and emotional reasons, but the difference is blurring. Powell (1987), reviewing the literature, found that gender did not significantly affect selection decisions, and that the greater the amount and relevance of information about the job and the applicant, the less gender-biased the decision. Governments have taken initiatives, mostly legislation, against discrimination; women are disproportionately represented in secretarial occupations and men in machine operative and craft work; a UK survey (Labour Market Trend, 2001) showed women earned 82 per cent of men's average hourly earnings in full-time employment. In India representation of women in employment is still poor though improving; banking, teaching and health care are traditionally preferred by women, who often prefer regulated working hours for work-life balance. The courseware cites the Equal Remuneration Act 1976 (equal remuneration and no gender discrimination), the Factories Act 1948 (permission for women to work odd hours with protection), the Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao programme and an amendment to the Hindu Succession Act 1956 giving daughters equal rights in ancestral property. On sexual harassment it reports the Supreme Court's directive and the Sexual Harassment of Women at Work Place (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act 2013 (the "PoSH Act"), passed by the Lok Sabha on 3 September 2012 and the Rajya Sabha on 26 February 2013, assented to on 23 April 2013 and in force from 9 December 2013, and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013 adding a sexual harassment offence to the Indian Penal Code; it states that employers must report such offences, and quotes a McKinsey 2021 report that women have made gains in representation, especially in senior leadership.

payload.title: What shapes behaviour at work: four groups of factors
payload.core_explanation_md:
Human behaviour is complex: it combines originating and responding behaviour, reflects a person's psychological make-up, and results from **biological, psychological and social** processes. **Employee behaviour** is how employees respond to specific circumstances at work.

Kurt Lewin's idea, as the courseware states it: behaviour is a **function of the person and the environment**. Neither alone explains it.

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Environmental** | Economic (employment level, wage rates, outlook); social (norms, cultural values, work ethic); political (stability, quality of the political system) |
| **Personal** | Age, sex, education, abilities, marital status, family background |
| **Organisational** | Nature of job, structure and design, leadership, compensation and reward system, growth opportunities, culture, facilities, personnel policies |
| **Psychological** | Personality, perception, attitudes, values, learning |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Two employees in the same bank can behave very differently in the same situation because the personal and psychological factors differ even when the organisational factors are identical.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four groups of factors the courseware gives for behaviour.

payload.title: Individual differences and changing views of "man"
payload.core_explanation_md:
Because people differ in needs and motives, **the same treatment will not motivate everyone**. If people were identical, standard rules and minimal judgement would do.

Managers' views of employees have changed:

| View | Idea | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Economic / rational man** | Motivated mainly by money | Ignores social needs |
| **Social man** (from the Hawthorne studies) | Wants to belong; treatment and recognition matter | Neglects the work itself; can be manipulative |
| **Creative man** (Argyris, Likert, McGregor) | Needs opportunities to use creativity and grow | Not everyone wants to grow on the job |
| **Complex man** (current view) | A complex being; personalities differ | Requires understanding individual personality |

Understanding personality helps managers **predict** behaviour such as absenteeism, turnover and work involvement, adjust their own behaviour, and take **preventive** steps in time.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This is why "one size fits all" HR policies underperform: they assume a single view of what people want from work.

self_check.prompt_text: Which view of employees holds that they are motivated mainly by money?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The economic or rational man view.

payload.title: Seven assumptions about behaviour at work
payload.core_explanation_md:
Technical competence is not enough: behaviour and **interpersonal skills** matter because people work in teams, and good teamwork creates **synergy**, an outcome greater than the sum of individual contributions.

The courseware lists seven basic assumptions about human behaviour at work:

| About people | About organisations |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Individuals **differ** | 5. Organisations are **social systems** |
| 2. The **whole person** matters | 6. There is **mutuality of interest** among members |
| 3. Behaviour is **caused** | 7. Organisational behaviour is **holistic** (combines 1 to 6) |
| 4. An individual has **dignity** | |

And a useful reminder: every person is in some respects **like all others**, **like some others** and **like no other**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The "like all others" level covers shared human traits; "like some others" covers groups such as introverts and extraverts or high and low risk takers; "like no other" is the individual's unique personality.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two of the seven assumptions concern organisations rather than people?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Organisations are social systems, and there is mutuality of interest among organisational members.

payload.title: Personality and the Type A and Type B profiles
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Personality** (Salvatore Maddi): a stable set of characteristics and tendencies that determine the commonalities and differences in people's psychological behaviour (thoughts, feelings, actions), with continuity in time. People do not change overnight; changes occur slowly.

Two classical views: **Cattell** (a pattern of **traits** that helps understand and predict behaviour; traits are permanent) and **Eysenck** (temperaments largely genetic; two primary dimensions, **extraversion** and **neuroticism**).

**Type A and Type B** (Friedman, Meyer, Rosenman):

| Type A | Type B |
| --- | --- |
| Restless, always moving, impatient | Easy going, relaxed about time pressure |
| Multitasks; starts a new task before finishing | Systematic and methodical |
| Squeezes more into less time | Plans so urgent matters are done on time |
| No time to relax | Balanced outlook on life; less competitive |

Both types are found among bank managers. The courseware describes a Type A manager as likely to have an untidy cabin and loses papers; a Type B manager works methodically.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: These are tendencies, not boxes. The value for a manager is predicting how a person is likely to react to deadlines, delegation and pressure.

self_check.prompt_text: Which type of personality is restless, impatient and often multitasks?

payload.title: Erikson's eight stages, and what they look like at work
payload.core_explanation_md:
Erikson described personality development as eight stages, each a tension between two outcomes. The courseware gives a workplace parallel for each:

| Stage | At work |
| --- | --- |
| 1. **Trust vs mistrust** | Depending on others for guidance; trust grows if they respond well |
| 2. **Autonomy vs shame and doubt** | Happy when functioning independently after induction; doubt after mistakes |
| 3. **Initiative vs guilt** | Taking initiative; guilt if resources are wasted |
| 4. **Industry vs inferiority** | Working hard for a place; low self-esteem if unsuccessful |
| 5. **Identity vs role confusion** | Proving oneself as a performing member; role identity may be diffused |
| 6. **Intimacy vs isolation** | Close contact at work or a sense of isolation |
| 7. **Generativity vs stagnation** | Developing others; stagnation if not |
| 8. **Integrity vs despair** | Near retirement: self-worth from achievements, or purposelessness |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Type A and B describe personality features; Erikson's model describes growth stages and their effects on mental personality. They answer different questions.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Erikson stage is linked to an employee near retirement who feels either self-worth or despair?

payload.title: Four theories of personality
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Theory | Core idea | Workplace illustration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Psychoanalytic** (Freud) | Personality = **id** (unconscious pleasure drive), **ego** (controls the id through reality), **super ego** (conscience, absorbed values). A balance among the three is needed | Over-strong super ego: guilt over trifles. Weak super ego: id runs loose. Daydreaming, forgetfulness, absenteeism, tardiness can be analysed this way |
| **Trait** | Traits are inherent, more heredity than environment | Describing people as aggressive, loyal, flexible, submissive |
| **Self-concept** (Carl Rogers) | Behaviour is consistent with the **image of oneself**, formed by interaction and feedback | A person with a self-image of high independence seeks challenge and recognition, not just pay or security |
| **Social learning** | Personality is mostly **learned** through reinforcement and punishment; person and environment interact | Praise reinforces good behaviour; frustration can reinforce aggression |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Positive feedback reinforces self-concept; negative feedback lowers self-regard and raises tension and anxiety, so feedback style affects development.

self_check.prompt_text: In Freud's scheme, which part acts as the conscience?

payload.title: The brain and Holland's personality-job fit
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware also links personality to the **brain**: through electrical stimulation of the brain (ESB) and **split-brain** psychology. As it summarises (and notes remains open to research):

| Left hemisphere (controls right side of body) | Right hemisphere (controls left side) |
| --- | --- |
| Speech and verbal, logical and mathematical, linear and detailed, sequential, analytic | Spatial and musical, holistic, artistic, emotional, intuitive and creative, simultaneous, facial recognition |

**Holland's personality-job fit theory:** satisfaction depends on how well personality matches the occupation. Six types:

| Type | Prefers | Examples of congruent jobs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Realistic** | Physical skills; shy, stable, practical | Mechanic, farmer |
| **Investigative** | Thinking, understanding; analytical, curious | Biologist, economist |
| **Social** | Helping others; sociable, friendly | Teacher, social worker |
| **Conventional** | Orderly, rule-regulated; efficient, unimaginative | Accountant, bank teller, file clerk |
| **Enterprising** | Influencing others; ambitious, self-confident | Lawyer, public relations specialist |
| **Artistic** | Creative, unsystematic; imaginative, emotional | Painter, musician, writer |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The practical message: a good match between personality and job raises satisfaction; a poor match raises dissatisfaction.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Holland type does the courseware pair with the job of bank teller?

payload.title: Diversity at work and the trap of homogeneous reproduction
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Diversity** includes race or ethnicity and gender (the most recognised), and also disability, family background, age, lifestyle and culture.

Traditional HR systems were built on **homogeneity**: recruit from the sources that produced past successes; hire, promote and evaluate people who resemble the decision-makers. The courseware calls this **homogeneous reproduction**: only those who fit the dominant coalition pass through. Mass aptitude tests selecting similar abilities create another risk: when that ability becomes obsolete the whole group becomes redundant. Its example: banks in the 1970s and 1980s recruited for numerical ability to run rapid branch expansion; computerisation made it obsolete, and banks now need selling and marketing skills.

**Why diversity helps:** complementary skills; well-managed diverse workgroups show more **creativity, problem solving, cohesiveness and communication**, and organisations gain in performance and quality of product and service.

**Why it often fails:** diversity programmes are introduced **piecemeal**, without a holistic view or integration with other systems, and laws change rules without changing culture and beliefs.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A diverse workforce is also a source of adaptability: the organisation can respond to market changes, new technology and shifts in expectations.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The tendency of selection and promotion to favour people like the decision-makers, letting through only those who fit the dominant coalition.

payload.title: Managing diversity: three approaches and four problems
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Three traditional HR approaches:**

| Approach | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Diversity enlargement** | Increases the **representation** of people from different ethnic and cultural backgrounds, changing demographic composition |
| **Diversity sensitivity** | **Trains** members about cultural differences to promote understanding |
| **Cultural audit** | **Surveys** to find what blocks non-traditional employees and how groups see the dominant culture; must link to HR systems, and should find similarities too |

**Problems:**

1. **Critical mass**: a few diverse recruits may feel isolated or like **tokens** (Kanter).
2. **Time**: it takes years for the organisation's profile to show the effort.
3. **Business conditions**: growth and frequent hiring speed progress; slow expansion or downsizing slows it.
4. **Piecemeal action** without integration with other HR systems.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A cultural audit is meant to be mutual: new culture and HR strategies should be designed so that all members can contribute their potential.

self_check.prompt_text: Which approach teaches employees about cultural differences through training?

payload.title: Gender issues at work: what the courseware reports
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware's account, as far as it is taught here:

- Some jobs have long been associated with a gender for physical, social or emotional reasons, but the difference is **blurring**.
- **Powell (1987)** found gender did not significantly affect selection decisions; the more relevant information an evaluator has about the job and applicant, the **less gender-biased** the decision.
- Pay gaps persist: a UK survey (2001) found women earned **82 per cent** of men's average hourly earnings in full-time work.
- In India, representation of women is improving but still poor; banking, teaching and health care have been preferred by women, who often want **regulated working hours** for work-life balance.
- **Sexual harassment:** the courseware reports the Supreme Court's directive and then the **PoSH Act 2013** (the Sexual Harassment of Women at Work Place (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act), in force from **9 December 2013**, and says employers must report sexual harassment offences.
- McKinsey (2021), as cited: women have made gains in representation, especially in senior leadership.

**Left out on purpose:** the courseware also cites older equal-pay, factory, succession and criminal-law provisions. They were not checked against the law in force at the 30 June 2026 cut-off (several have since been replaced or reorganised), so this course does not teach them. Verify any such provision from current sources before relying on it.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The idea to keep: gender should not decide selection or pay, women need workplaces that respect safety and work-life balance, and employers carry a duty to prevent and report harassment.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Act do the courseware and the Supreme Court's directive lead to on sexual harassment at the workplace?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Work Place (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act 2013, the "PoSH Act".

The courseware attributes theories and findings to named authors (Kurt Lewin, Maddi, Cattell, Eysenck, Friedman, Meyer and Roseman, Erikson, Freud, Carl Rogers, John Holland, Kanter 1977, Powell 1987, a UK 2001 labour market survey, McKinsey 2021); none was checked against the original work.

The courseware's account of Indian law on gender (Equal Remuneration Act 1976, Factories Act 1948, Hindu Succession Act 1956 as amended, the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013 and its 2016 amendment note, and section 354 of the Indian Penal Code added by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013) is its own and was NOT checked against primary sources or against the cut-off date of 30 June 2026. Some of these have since been replaced or reorganised (for example the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, in force from 1 July 2024, and the wage and factories laws by the labour codes); the items therefore attribute the statements to the courseware, avoid asking for section numbers or penalties, and the ledger records the limit.
The courseware's statement that the proposed 33 per cent representation of women in Parliament was pending reflects its writing date; it is not used in questions.
The courseware's table of the left and right brain hemispheres is said by the courseware to be open to research; it is taught only as the courseware's summary.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.
